newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Toyota targets 3 pct Europen share.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Toyota targets 3 pct Europen share.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp's European arm has set itself an ambitious target of three percent of the region's vehicle market in 1997, compared with a 2.6 percent share in 1996, company executives said on Wednesday.
The Japanese carmaker's plan, based on a stated growth strategy meant to generate record sales around the globe this year, came despite its forecast of slow European market growth.

Speaking at a presentation in London, Toyota Motor Europe (TME) managing director Tatsuo Takahashi said its sales target of 450,000 vehicles, up more than nine percent on 1996, was set against an expectation that the market would grow by between two and three percent to total nearly 15 million units in 1997.
"If we reach 450,000 within this forecast market then we can reach 3.0 percent of the market, that is our target," a senior company spokesman explained.

Last year's final European sales figure of about 412,000 vehicles separated into about 330,000 Toyota passenger cars, including the popular RAV4 four-wheel drive range. The remainder were pure commercial vehicles, primarily vans.

Haruyuki Miyadai, of TME's Brussels head office, said that the Toyota market share in Europe was roughly the same for commercial vehicles and passenger vehicles, but that 1997 growth would be concentrated on cars.
Two 1996-launched imported car models, which have yet to feed into the market place in substantial volumes partly due to heavy demand in Japan, are expected to fuel the rise.
One of these, the medium-sized Picnic people carrier, is expected to add about 16,000 sales in 1997 compared with just 2,000 in its first few months of selling in 1996, Miyadai said.

The other, a new medium-sized Landcruiser four-wheel drive car known in Britain as the Colorado, was only launched in Europe last September and has already built up a significant order backlog, he added.

In all, Toyota introduced six new car models in the region in 1996, including a new Starlet small car. TME vice chairman Alan Marsh said the company would have "another extensive model programme" in 1997, but he gave no details.
By the third or fourth quarter of 1998 Toyota expects to have started production of its latest top-selling Corolla car at its only European plant in Derby, England, alongside the Carina.

TME director Brian Jackson said that although production volumes for 1998 and beyond had not yet been finalised, 1997 would see 117,000 cars made at Derby for the second year in a row. As the new project is completed, the number of people employed should rise to 3,000 from 2,300 at present.
The head of Toyota's British manufacturing company, Toshio Mizushima, said that the company currently had no plans to produce a third model in Britain.
Arch-rival Nissan Motor Co's announced this week it planned to open a third product line at its Sunderland in northeast England.
